titulo.texto: Recreation of the Traditional Maya Homestead and House

frase_gancho.texto: A palm-thatched house and a garden where the whole Maya world fits.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the house and its yard we move on to a wall painting. Look for the mural signed by Rafael Coronel, whose title speaks of the spiritual world of the Maya of the Yucatán Peninsula.

guion_corto.texto: This is a Maya house from Yucatán, rebuilt at full scale. Notice its shape: an oval floor plan with rounded corners, walls of poles and clay, and a very tall palm roof that lets the air flow through and keeps the interior cool. Inside there are hammocks, a comal, a metate, and a small family altar. But the house cannot be understood without the solar, the plot of land that surrounds it: fruit trees, vegetables, and medicinal plants grow there, there are hives of a stingless bee, and everything is enclosed by a low stone wall called an albarrada. For the Maya family, house and solar form a single unit: there they live, eat, heal, and pray.

guion_largo.texto:
This house is not a scale model: according to what is told, it was built in the museum by Maya builders who came from Yucatán, using the traditional materials and techniques, when the ethnography halls were set up in the early 1960s. That is why, as you step in, you can almost smell the dry straw and the wood. It is a house made by people who know how to live in it.

The oval shape has a practical reason. Without corners, the wind goes around the house instead of pushing against it, and it is said to withstand the hurricanes of the peninsula better. The palm roof stays in good condition thanks to the smoke from the hearth, which drives away insects. And the heat escapes through the top, so it is cool inside. It is an example of architecture that adapts to the climate without needing any machines.

It also carries a meaning. The four main posts hold up the roof, and it has been interpreted that they recall the four bacabes, the beings who, according to Maya myth, held up the four corners of the sky. Perhaps you remember the idea of the four directions in the flower of the Huastec quechquémitl: here it appears again, now in the form of a house. To live inside it is to live inside a small, ordered universe.

Look at the hammock. The word comes from Taíno, the language of the Caribbean islands, and it is one of the many that Spanish took from the Americas. Sleeping in it lifts you off the ground, away from the damp and from scorpions, and by day it is gathered up to leave the space free. The Maya house changes its use with the hours: at night it is a bedroom, and by day it is a kitchen, a workshop, and a place for visits.

Let us step out into the solar. It is the family’s pantry and pharmacy. There are fruit trees, vegetables, and healing herbs, and among them the chaya, a green leaf that is cooked like spinach. There are also hens and pigs, a well, and walls of stone laid without mortar, the albarradas, which mark the boundaries and shelter the yard from the wind. Everything is put to use, and what is left over returns to the earth.

And then there are the bees. The Maya have raised a stingless bee for centuries, which in their language is called Xunaan Kab, «the lady bee». It lives in hollow logs, and its honey, scarce and intense in flavor, is used as food and as medicine. Today there are families who continue to care for it so that it is not lost, and with it they also look after a way of living together with the forest.

It is said that in the solar and in the milpa live the aluxes, small beings who watch over the field, and who are sometimes left a gourd cup of atole to keep them happy. And behind it all is the milpa, the field of corn, beans, and squash that you saw in the first hall upstairs. Without it, the house and the solar would not hold together.

When the rain is late, the Cha Chaak is held, a ceremony to ask for it. It takes place in the field, with an altar of branches, corn breads, and ritual drinks, and it is led by a specialist who prays in the Maya language. The god who is addressed is Chaac, the same one on the [Kabah mask](mna_s09_mascaron_chaac) that you saw downstairs, a relative of [Cocijo](mna_s07_urna_cocijo) and of Tláloc. It is the clearest proof that the Maya world did not remain only in stone: it still asks for water, with respect, so that the milpa will grow.

texto: Notice the oval shape of the house and its palm roof
Find the hammock, the comal, and the metate inside the house
Observe the low stone wall that encloses the solar

texto.Region: Yucatán Peninsula (Campeche, Yucatán and Quintana Roo)
texto.Technique/Material: Vernacular architecture (hardwood, wattle and daub, huano palm, henequen)
texto.Function: Recreation of the traditional dwelling and the biocultural space of the family homestead plot

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Maya house is a primitive shelter.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Its oval shape, its tall roof, and its solar with a garden are designed for the heat, the wind, and the life of an entire family.
